industrial-revolution-s1.title: Three early industrial regions of Europe

map.label: Reference map of Europe marking three early industrial regions on coalfields: A, Manchester in England; B, the Ruhr in Germany; C, Upper Silesia in Poland
map.legendTitle: Countries with a marked early industrial region of the 1800s. Each sits on a coalfield: A Manchester, B Ruhr, C Upper Silesia

industrial-revolution-s2.title: Workers in Country A by kind of work, 1800 to 1900

plot.label: Line chart of Country A, 1800 to 1900: the share of workers in farming falls from 75% to 20% while the share in factories and mines rises from 10% to 45%, passing farming between 1860 and 1880

items.q: The legend says each marked region sits on a coalfield. Why did early factories cluster in places like these?
options: Coal fueled the steam engines
Coalfields were where the best farmland was found
Rulers kept factories away from the coast by law
Each region held its country's capital city

why.correct: Steam engines ran on coal, which was bulky and expensive to move by land in the 1800s, so factories located near the coalfields.
options: Right: steam engines burned coal, and coal was heavy and costly to haul, so mills located on top of it.
Coal lies under many kinds of land; farmland was not what drew mills to these four regions.
No such ban existed; Upper Silesia and the Ruhr are far inland.
Manchester, the Ruhr towns and Upper Silesia are not capitals. Their pull was coal, not government.

items.q: At what scale of analysis does this map show early industrial regions?
options: Regional: places in several countries of Europe
Local: one neighborhood inside one single city
Global: the whole world shown at once on one map
National: one country and its many provinces

why.correct: The scale of analysis is the scale of the data shown: three places across several countries of Europe make a regional scale.
options: Right: the data are four places across several European countries, so the scale is regional.
The marks are spread across three countries, not within one city.
Only Europe is shown, so the map works at a regional scale, not a global one.
Three countries are marked, so it is wider than one national scale.

items.q: Manchester, marked A on the map, grew from a market town into a large factory city in the early 1800s. Which explanation of that growth includes every link?
options: Mills on the coalfield needed workers, so farmworkers moved in
Manchester grew larger because it was an industrial place in England
Farmworkers moved away from Manchester to farm land in colonies
Its birth rate rose sharply after its mills shut down

why.correct: An explain answer gives every link: mills on the coalfield needed labor, so rural workers moved to Manchester for factory wages, so the city grew.
options: Right: a cause (mills on the coal), a link (the need for workers) and an effect (migration into the city).
This restates the idea without the link: why industry made the city grow is missing.
That would shrink the city, not grow it.
The mills did not close in this period, and the growth came mostly from people moving in.

items.q: According to the chart, between which years did the share of workers in factories and mines first pass the share in farming?

why.correct: Read both lines at each year: the factory line crosses above the farming line between 1860 and 1880.
options: Right: in 1860 farming (42%) was still ahead of factories (33%); by 1880 factories (40%) had passed farming (30%).
In 1820 farming was 68% and factories only 15%, so farming was far ahead.
In 1860 farming (42%) was still above factories (33%).
Factories had already passed farming by 1880 (40% to 30%).

items.q: Which statement best describes the trend the chart shows for Country A over the whole century?
options: Work shifted from farms to factories and mines
Farming and factory work both grew at the same pace
Factory work peaked in 1840 and then fell back again
Most workers in 1900 still farmed, just as in 1800

why.correct: A describe answer names what changed, the direction and how much: farming fell by about 55 points while factory work rose by 35.
options: Right: farming fell from 75% to 20% while factory and mine work rose from 10% to 45%.
The two lines move in opposite directions: farming falls while factory work rises.
The factory line rises in every period, reaching 45% in 1900.
In 1900 only 20% farmed; 45% worked in factories and mines.

items.q: Which outcome is most likely in Country A as the chart's trend goes on?
options: Towns grow as rural people take factory jobs
Cities empty out as factory workers go back to farms
Farm output drops to zero as farmworkers leave
People spread out evenly across the countryside

why.correct: Factories are in towns, so a shift of workers into factories brings rural-to-urban migration and urban growth.
options: Right: factory jobs are in towns, so rural-to-urban migration and growing cities follow.
The chart shows the opposite flow: workers leaving farming.
Fewer farmworkers can still grow plenty of food with new machines; 20% still farm in 1900.
Factories cluster in towns, so people concentrate rather than spread out.

items.q: Which is a limitation of the chart for studying industrialization inside Country A?
options: One national share hides which regions changed first
It uses invented data, so it shows no clear trend over time
It covers too many years for a reader to see a trend
It counts workers, so it hides change from year to year

why.correct: A national share is one number for the whole country, so it hides the regional and local pattern of where factories opened.
options: Right: national data hide differences between regions; a coalfield region may have changed decades before a farming region.
Invented data still show a trend; the limit is what the scale of the data can and cannot reveal.
Six points across a century is enough to read a trend.
The lines change across the years, so change over time is shown.

items.q: Great Britain was the first place to industrialize, in the late 1700s. Which combination best explains why?
options: New machines plus coal, iron and trade wealth
The largest population of any country in the world then
A law against farming that pushed people into towns
A warm climate that suited factory work year-round

why.correct: Technology (spinning machines, the steam engine) and resources (coal, iron ore, capital from trade) came together in Britain first.
options: Right: industrialization needs both new technology and the resources to run it, and Britain had both.
Britain was not the most populous country; China and India had far more people.
There was no ban; new farm methods simply needed fewer workers.
Climate was not the cause; technology and resources were.

items.q: How did the steam engine change where factories could be built?
options: Mills could leave rivers and cluster in towns near coal
Mills moved next to waterfalls so the engines stayed cool
Factories were allowed in capital cities and nowhere else
Factories spread out evenly across the whole countryside

why.correct: Before steam, a water wheel needed a fast stream. Steam engines ran on coal anywhere, so factories moved to towns near coal, workers and buyers.
options: Right: water wheels tied mills to streams; steam power let them move to towns.
This reverses the change: steam freed mills from rivers.
Steam power let factories locate in many towns, near coal and workers.
They clustered in towns and on coalfields rather than spreading out.

items.q: Why did industrialization in the 1800s increase European control over colonies in Africa and Asia?
options: Factories needed raw materials and new buyers
European factories ran short of workers and wanted farmland
Colonies had already built more factories than Europe
European governments wanted to slow their own factories

why.correct: Machines that make goods quickly need raw materials quickly and buyers for the goods, so industrial powers sought control of places that could supply both.
options: Right: the search for raw materials (cotton, rubber, palm oil) and markets fed colonialism and imperialism.
The pull was raw materials and markets, not farmland for European factory workers.
Most colonies had few factories; they mainly supplied raw materials.
Governments backed factory growth; control of colonies helped it.

items.q: Britain industrialized in the late 1700s mainly through private mill owners. Japan began after 1868 with its government bringing in foreign machines and advisers. What does this difference show?
options: Later places could industrialize by a state-led route
Japan copied British laws and policies one by one
Japanese industry started without machines or power
Later industrializers had little need for raw materials

why.correct: The ingredients stayed the same, but a later industrializer such as Japan used government planning to catch up quickly.
options: Right: the same mix of machines, power and resources arrived by a different route in a later place.
Japan adapted industry to its own goals rather than copying Britain law by law.
Japan imported machines and built power, the same ingredients Britain used.
Japan, too, needed raw materials such as coal and cotton.

items.q: Which were effects of industrialization in Britain in the 1800s? Select all that apply.
options: A large urban working class that earned wages in factories
Rapid growth of mill towns, with crowded housing
A move of most people back to farms in the countryside
A sharp drop in trade with other continents
Fewer goods made, at higher prices

why.correct: Industrialization created a working class and fast-growing, crowded cities, while trade and output grew.
options: Right: factory jobs created a new class of wage workers in cities.
Right: towns such as Manchester grew fast, with crowding and disease.
The movement was from farms to towns, not the other way.
Trade grew: mills needed raw cotton from abroad and sold cloth worldwide.
Machines made more goods, more cheaply.

items.q: Put the steps of the Industrial Revolution in Britain in cause-and-effect order, first to last.
options: New machines and steam power are invented
Factories open in towns near coal
Farmworkers move to towns for factory jobs
Cities grow quickly and crowd up

why.correct: Technology came first, then factories in towns, then the migration of workers, then fast and crowded urban growth.

items.q: An invented mill town in Country A had 20,000 people in 1800 and 140,000 people in 1850. By what percent did its population grow? (Invented data for practice.)

why.correct: Percent change is (new minus old) divided by old, times 100: $\frac{140{,}000 - 20{,}000}{20{,}000} \times 100 = 600\%$.

mistakes.why: That is the new size as a percent of the old (700%). Growth subtracts the old value first: (140,000 minus 20,000) over 20,000, times 100.
You divided by the new value. Percent change divides the change by the old value, 20,000.

items.q: Build an explanation of how the Industrial Revolution changed one city, naming the place and the scale.

why.correct: A full explanation names a real place, its scale, and the link from mills to migration to growth.

specific.frame: At the ___ scale, in ___, steam mills needed many workers, so ___.
specific.model: At the local scale, in Manchester, England, steam mills needed many workers, so farmworkers moved in for wages and the city grew quickly.

scale.label: Scale of analysis
options: local
global

why.1: One city is the local scale; the global scale is the whole world.

place.label: Place
options: Manchester, England
many places in Europe

why.1: Name one real place: readers give no credit for a vague place.

effect.label: Effect
options: farmworkers moved in for wages and the city grew quickly
the city grew

why.1: "The city grew" leaves out the link: say who moved and why.

items.q: British cloth made in steam mills was sold cheaply in India in the 1800s. What was one effect on India?
options: India's hand weavers lost buyers and work
India soon built more steam mills than Britain had
India stopped growing cotton for export to Britain
Indian weavers moved to Manchester to run its mills

why.correct: Cheap machine-made imports undercut hand weavers, so industry in one place could shrink work in another.
options: Right: cheap factory cloth undercut India's hand weaving, a cost of industrialization felt in a colony.
Britain led in mills in this period; India mainly supplied raw cotton.
India kept growing cotton, much of it for British mills.
There was no large migration of weavers from India to run British mills.
